title: Child care assistance (CCDF subsidies) by state
methodology: One record per state and DC for the state's child care subsidy program funded by the federal Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF). Program names, agencies and apply pages come from each state's own site, cross-checked against the state listings on Childcare.gov (ACF), and were checked on October 9, 2026. Every state runs a program, so every record is marked covered. Income limits are the entry limit for a family of three: the most recent figure we found in the state's own published chart, or in the National Women's Law Center's 2025 survey of state administrators (policies as of February 2025, with changes reported through late 2025). Each limit carries its own as-of month and, where the source gives one, its basis (a share of state median income or of the federal poverty level). The February 2025 NWLC figures are kept for every state for comparison. Copay figures are the highest monthly copay for a family of three as a share of income that each state reported in its FFY 2025-2027 CCDF plan (ACF, January 2025), replaced by a later stated cap where a state announced one. States that had a temporary federal waiver from the 7% rule and reported a figure at or under 7% are left blank, because the plan figure may not have applied to every family. Waiting-list status is NWLC's February 2025 count, replaced by a state announcement where one was newer. Job-search eligibility at application is from NWLC's 2025 survey. The 7% federal copay requirement was rescinded effective July 13, 2026, so copay rules may change after the dates shown.

ccdfBasics.text: The Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) is the main federal source of money that helps families pay for child care. Every state and DC runs a subsidy program with it: the state pays part of the cost to the provider you choose, and you pay a copay based on your income and family size.

federalEligibility.text: Under federal law, a child under 13 can qualify when family income is no more than 85% of state median income and the parents are working or attending job training or school. Children in protective services can also qualify. States can set lower income limits, and most do.

medianIncomeLimitPctSmi2025.text: In February 2025, the middle state's limit for a family of three was 60% of state median income.
medianIncomeLimitPctSmi2025.note: Median of NWLC's percent-of-median-income figures for the 50 states and DC; Colorado's county range is excluded.

copayRule2024.text: A 2024 HHS rule, effective April 30, 2024, required states to keep family copays at or below 7% of income. Some states got temporary waivers to comply later.

copayRule2026.text: HHS rescinded the 7% copay requirement in a final rule published May 12, 2026, effective July 13, 2026. States now set their own sliding fee scales, as long as copays aren't a barrier to getting help, and can keep a 7% cap if they choose. HHS isn't recommending a new benchmark.

copayCap7AcfCount.text: As of March 2026, 31 states and DC limited copays to 7% of income or less, according to ACF's review of state CCDF plans: 15 states and DC at 7%, and 16 states below it.

copayCap7Computed.text: Counted from the state records in this file: states whose most recent copay figure we found is at or below 7% of income.

waitlists2025.text: Seventeen states had waiting lists or frozen intake in February 2025, up from 13 a year earlier, with about 225,500 children on waiting lists, a 90% increase.

headStart.text: Head Start and Early Head Start programs can't charge eligible families a fee to take part. A pregnant woman or child qualifies with family income at or below the poverty line, or if the family is eligible for public assistance such as TANF, the child is homeless or the child is in foster care. Programs can enroll some families above those lines.

providerChargesAboveCopay.text: In 40 states, a provider whose price is above the state's subsidy payment may charge you the difference on top of your copay. Ask before you enroll.

taxBreaks2026.text: For 2026, a dependent care FSA through your employer can shelter up to $7,500 of child care costs from tax, and the Child and Dependent Care Credit pays up to 50% of up to $3,000 in expenses for one child or $6,000 for two or more. The same dollars can't count for both.
